title: Pseudorandom generators from hitting-set generators
formal:
Does the existence of a polynomial-time hitting-set generator secure against all polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply the existence of a polynomial-time pseudorandom generator secure against all such circuits, in the cryptographic regime defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists H\;\operatorname{HSG}(H)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists G\;\operatorname{PRG}(G)\bigr).
\]
Both generators must be uniform, have a seed shorter than their output, and meet their respective security conditions with negligible error. Their seed lengths, negligible functions and polynomial running-time bounds may differ. This is an implication between existence statements; it does not require an algorithm that compiles a given hitting-set generator into a pseudorandom generator.

why: This asks whether hitting dense sets and reproducing acceptance probabilities have the same existential power when a uniform efficient generator must withstand arbitrarily stronger polynomial-size tests. Pseudorandom generators are foundational cryptographic objects connected to one-way functions, while the weaker hitting guarantee arises naturally from errorless average-case hardness. A resolution would clarify whether these two notions represent distinct assumptions about computational randomness, rather than merely improve the parameters of one construction.
status_note: The selected cryptographic question is explicitly open in Santhanam 2020 and is highlighted again in the 2022 source. The 2022 positive theorem has seed-prefix and NC1/poly restrictions. The checked 2023 conditional equivalence and 2024–2026 results use different assumptions, adversaries or targets. Individual primary-source reading and a bounded later-work search completed on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated existence implication. This supports a dated source-open classification, not a claim of exhaustive current verification.

progress.text: Santhanam explicitly asks whether HSGs and PRGs are equivalent in the cryptographic regime. Section 2.2 fixes the default security error to negligible, the generator time to a fixed polynomial in output length, and the tests to arbitrary polynomial-size circuits.

Hirahara and Santhanam revisit the question and prove Theorem 28 for seed-extending generators against \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\), meaning nonuniform polynomial-size Boolean circuits of logarithmic depth. That special case is distinct from the unrestricted polynomial-size test class of this card.

Under the Meta-Complexity Padding Conjecture, Hirahara proves related equivalences involving HSGs, PRGs and one-way functions against uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms with infinitely-often security. The conditional hypothesis, adversary model and length quantifiers differ from the present target.

importance.reason: Individually assessed as a foundational equivalence question about cryptographic pseudorandomness: it compares two natural security primitives and bears directly on the gap between errorless and error-prone average-case hardness and on the role of one-way functions. The selected statement is about unrestricted polynomial-size Boolean tests, not a narrow generator family or a parameter optimization. The score is editorial judgment based on these connections and the precise source questions, replacing the inherited unassessed midpoint.

sentences: A hitting-set generator produces strings that intersect every sufficiently dense set accepted by a polynomial-size Boolean circuit.
A pseudorandom generator must instead approximate every such circuit’s acceptance probability when its seed is chosen uniformly.

The selected cryptographic question asks whether the existence of the first kind of uniform polynomial-time generator entails the existence of the second, with negligible security bounds and any nontrivial stretch.
The generators may have different parameters, and the known seed-extending result for logarithmic-depth circuits does not establish the unrestricted implication.
A complete Lean proof must decide this existence implication, clarifying the relationship between two basic forms of computational randomness.

definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge 0\), let \(U_m\) denote the uniform distribution on the \(2^m\) binary strings of length \(m\). Output lengths are integers \(N\ge 2\). An admissible generator family \(F=(F_N)_{N\ge 2}\) has a seed-length function \(s:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N\) with \(1\le s(N)<N\) and maps \(F_N:\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\to\{0,1\}^{N}\). One deterministic multitape Turing machine computes \(s(N)\) from \(1^N\), and another computes \(F_N(z)\) from \((1^N,z)\) for every seed \(z\). Here \(1^N\) is the unary encoding of \(N\). There are constants \(A,b\ge 1\), depending only on the family, such that each computation takes at most \(A(N+1)^b\) steps. In particular, time is polynomial in the output length. A machine has finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes with a fixed finite alphabet. In one step each head reads and may move by at most one cell, each work head may write one symbol, and at most one output bit may be appended. All tapes start at their first cell and are indexed by nonnegative integers; a left move at zero stays at zero. The generator input is the literal string \(1^N\#z\), and the seed-length output is the binary encoding of \(s(N)\). The machine programs and tape counts are independent of \(N\). These machines receive no advice, oracle or randomness. The output need not contain the seed, and different seeds may have the same output.

A test at length \(N\) is an arbitrary deterministic Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{N}\to\{0,1\}\), with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, constant gates, unrestricted fan-out and unrestricted depth. Its size is its number of gates, excluding the input nodes. There is no uniformity requirement on tests at different lengths. Security against polynomial-size circuits means the quantifier \(\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\) followed by a threshold length that may depend on \(c\), and then a guarantee for every circuit of size at most \(N^c\) at every larger length.

A function \(\nu:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to(0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge 1\) there is an integer \(N_a\) such that \(\nu(N)\le N^{-a}\) for all \(N\ge N_a\). No computability assumption is imposed on a security-bound function.

For an admissible family \(H\) with seed length \(s\), the property \(\operatorname{HSG}(H)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists N_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge N_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\ge\varepsilon(N)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\; C(H_N(z))=1.
\]
The hit is an existence guarantee; it need not occur with any specified fraction of seeds.

For an admissible family \(G\) with its own seed length \(t\), the property \(\operatorname{PRG}(G)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\eta\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists M_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge M_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{t(N)}}[C(G_N(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\eta(N).
\]
Thus generated outputs are sampled by a uniform seed, with multiplicity when seeds collide. The same generator and the same negligible function must serve every circuit-size exponent. In the implication, all generator, seed-length, time-bound and security-bound witnesses are existentially quantified separately on the two sides.
answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated existence implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish the existence of a generator satisfying the full PRG definition whenever a generator satisfying the HSG definition exists. A negative answer must establish that an HSG as defined exists while no PRG as defined exists, in the stated ordinary model. A theorem restricted to a smaller test class, additional hardness assumptions, infinitely many lengths, or the impossibility of a particular conversion method does not decide this implication.

context_blocks.text: A hitting-set generator guarantees that every sufficiently dense efficiently recognizable set contains at least one generated string. A pseudorandom generator controls each test's acceptance probability under a uniformly selected seed. The question asks whether the first kind of efficiently generated object already entails the existence of the second.

The 2022 source raises a broad conversion question in its introduction and footnote 2. This card explicitly selects the cryptographic existence question stated earlier as Question 6 in Santhanam's 2020 paper, which the 2022 discussion cites. The defaults in Section 2.2 of that paper specify polynomial time in output length, arbitrary polynomial-size circuit tests and negligible error. The seed may have any nontrivial length; neither a prescribed stretch nor preservation of parameters is part of the target. Unary output-length input and polynomial-time computation of the seed length make the uniform-family convention explicit.

The 2022 paper proves a different positive result for seed-extending generators tested by polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. Seed-extending means that the seed is a prefix of the output. The restrictions on both generator form and test class are part of that theorem. It does not settle the cryptographic implication above.

checked_sources: Read the full canonical TCS-5341 and the saved ITCS2022 source record, then checked the actual primary PDF rather than relying on the inherited 25-word excerpt. Read the introduction, especially PDF pages 2–4, Definition 26 on page 20 and Theorem 28 with its proof on page 21. The footnote raises the general conversion issue, the surrounding text distinguishes exponential time in seed length from polynomial-time generators, and the theorem only proves a seed-extending NC1/poly case. The theorem is not a solution for unrestricted P/poly adversaries. Cached as hsg-prg-hirahara-santhanam2022.pdf/.txt.

Read Santhanam ITCS2020 Question 6 on PDF page 3, density/fooling/hitting definitions in Section 2.1 on page 10, and all generator defaults in Section 2.2 on page 11. The explicit defaults are negligible error 1/N^{omega(1)}, a single fixed polynomial in output length for the generator, arbitrary polynomial-size nonuniform distinguishers, and seed length K(N)<N. Question 4 concerns stretching and is separate from Question 6. The public context discloses selection of this precise cryptographic regime from the broader 2022 footnote, rather than attributing all these parameters to the footnote itself. Cached as hsg-prg-santhanam2020.pdf/.txt. Publisher date confirmed as 6 January 2020.

Read the actual Hirahara ECCC TR23-037 report, dated 27 March 2023 and published 28 March, particularly Theorem 1.5 and Proposition 1.6 on printed pages 6–7/PDF 9–10 and the formal Theorem 11.7 on printed pages 56–57/PDF 59–60. Its equivalences assume the Meta-Complexity Padding Conjecture; HSG item 6 asks for seed n^{epsilon} for every positive constant epsilon, tests are uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms, and security is infinitely often. Proposition 1.6 derives the conjecture from already-existing nonuniform-secure one-way functions, so it does not remove the needed assumption when trying to derive one-way functions from a bare HSG. Cached as hsg-prg-padding2023.pdf/.txt.

Read Hirahara, Non-Disjoint Promise Problems from Meta-Computational View of Pseudorandom Generator Constructions, Theory of Computing 19(4), DOI 10.4086/toc.2023.v019.a004, actual PDF introduction and generator discussion (PDF pages 1–4 and 8). Received 18 August 2020, revised 26 September 2022, published 14 October 2023. It studies meta-computational hardness and generator constructions in different regimes and does not supply the selected uniform cryptographic HSG-to-PRG implication. Cached as hsg-prg-hirahara2023.pdf/.txt.

Read the actual Tzameret–Zhang ITCS2024 article 95, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2024.95: abstract, introductory definitions/context, Section 2.1 on PDF page 6 and Proposition 26 and Theorem 28 statements on page 7. Its sublinear stretching result is for demi-bits secure against nondeterministic adversaries, with a related HSG characterization against NP/poly. The paper explicitly still distinguishes demi-bits from super-bits. This neither converts arbitrary deterministic-test HSGs into PRGs nor refutes the existence implication. Cached as hsg-prg-demibits2024.pdf/.txt.

Read the 2020 Hirahara–Watanabe primary publisher abstract, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2020.15: its limit concerns nonadaptive randomized black-box reductions from hard languages to HSG security, not the nonexistence of an unrestricted existential implication. Read the ECCC2025/104 author abstract for Korten–Santhanam, which uses additional hardness assumptions and small-advice tests; the 2025 algebraic and restricted branching-program results were also distinguished from arbitrary Boolean circuits.

Read the primary ECCC TR26-178 abstract, submitted 6 September and published 13 September 2026, concerning HSGs for read-once CNFs with parities and width-3 ordered read-once branching programs. Root independently read Santhanam 2020 actual PDF pages 3, 10 and 11: Question 6 and all generator definitions/defaults support the selected cryptographic regime. The card separately quantifies the two families and allows collisions. Requiring positive negligible thresholds is harmless: zero or tiny bounds can be increased to positive negligible functions, and PRG-to-HSG uses a strictly larger negligible density threshold. Fixed multitape bit steps and literal unary-length delimiter encoding were added to state the uniform model completely.
